title: Ms. Y & Children’s Health Ireland (CHI)
text:
Decision
Ms. Y & Children’s Health Ireland (CHI)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200043-A0A0D3
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether CHI was justified in refusing access to further records relating to the applicant’s son under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act
9 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 28 October 2025, the applicant sought access to all records relating to her son from December 2024 to the date of her request.
In a decision dated 14 November 2025, CHI part-granted the applicant’s request. It refused access to parts of her son’s healthcare file under section 15(1)(i)(i) as these records had previously been provided to her. However, it released a number of additional records to the applicant which had been created since it previously provided her son’s medical record to her.
On 8 December 2025 the applicant sought an internal review of CHI’s decision. In her request for an internal review, the applicant argued that her son’s medical records were only a portion of the records sought.
In a letter dated 19 December 2025, CHI affirmed its original decision to refuse access to records under section 15(1)(i)(i).
On 5 January 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of CHI’s decision.
Upon receipt of the applicant’s application to this Office, the Investigating Officer sought clarification from the applicant on the scope of her request and her application for a review by this Office. By response on 1 June 2026, the applicant said she is not seeking a review of the records already released to her by CHI under the Data Protection Act 2018 and confirmed that these records were in her possession. She clarified that she would prefer to limit the scope of her application to any further records falling within the scope of her request outside of what may be considered her son’s medical records. She identified a number of records that she believes ought to exist, such as internal and external correspondence from the relevant time period and which relate to her son.
After clarifying the scope of the applicant’s request, the Investigating Officer invited CHI to make submissions justifying its decision on the applicant’s request. CHI said it did not wish to make any submissions on the matter.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence as outlined above. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
I note that the applicant is of the view that further records relating to her request ought to exist in addition to those records which were provided to her following a Subject Access Request (SAR) under GDPR legislation. In essence, although not explicitly relied upon to refuse access to records, this case involves a search issue under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act. I further note the applicant does not dispute that she received records relating to her son under a separate access regime to the FOI Act and has excluded those records from the scope of this review.
Accordingly, this review is concerned solely with whether CHI was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for further records relating to her son under section 15(1)(a) on the basis that further records do not exist or cannot be found after it took all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain the whereabouts of same.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. We have regard to the relevant information available and assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether CHI has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the records sought by the applicant.
It is important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “de novo", which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of my decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision.
As noted above, CHI did not provide this Office with any submissions in support of its decision, nor did it address any of the queries put to it by the Investigating Officer with respect to the searches it had conducted for records relevant to the applicant’s request. I therefore have no information before me on which to base a finding that it has carried out all reasonable steps to search for and provide the relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, having regard to the information before this Office, and in the absence of any submissions from the FOI Body in this case, I simply cannot find that CHI has taken all reasonable steps to locate further records sought by the applicant. In the circumstances, I find that CHI was not justified in refusing access to further records, under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no further records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
While I am under no obligation to do so, I would strongly encourage the parties to engage with one another to determine the precise records the applicant believes ought to exist.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul CHI’s decision. I find that CHI was not justified in refusing access to further records under section 15(1)(a) on the basis that further records do not exist or cannot be found after having taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of same and direct it to consider the matter afresh.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
